title: Jeff Bezos Pushes Amazon's Prime Video Toward an AI-First Overhaul
excerpt: A tense internal presentation led Bezos to demand that Prime Video's next redesign showcase Amazon's AI capabilities to its 200-million-plus user base.
body:
• Amazon founder Jeff Bezos pushed Prime Video head Mike Hopkins to overhaul the streaming service with AI at its core, according to Reuters.
  • The internal project, codenamed Lighthouse, would use AI to transform content recommendations and the homepage for 200 million-plus users.
  • The initiative grew from a contentious presentation last autumn in which Bezos was displeased with the lack of AI integration in Prime Video's plans.
  • Amazon is looking to Lighthouse as a showcase for its AI capabilities as competitors like OpenAI and Anthropic race ahead.

Jeff Bezos has identified Amazon's Prime Video as a high-profile platform to showcase the company's artificial intelligence capabilities, pushing the streaming service's leadership to put AI front and centre in a sweeping redesign, according to a Reuters report citing four people with direct knowledge of the matter.

The resulting effort, known internally as Lighthouse, would bring AI-driven features to the more than 200 million consumers who use Prime Video — making it one of the most visible consumer-facing applications of Amazon's AI investments to date.

A Presentation That Turned Contentious

The initiative traces its origins to an internal presentation last autumn in which Prime Video executives laid out their plans to update the streaming service. Bezos was displeased, the sources said, finding that the proposals from Prime Video head Mike Hopkins failed to sufficiently highlight AI and personalisation capabilities.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=Yl68RTGaNt8

"One option discussed by executives includes AI-driven tiles with pre-populated viewing suggestions such as "action movies from the 1980s" or "Christmas rom-coms," according to three of the sources."

The meeting became contentious, and Bezos pushed Hopkins to go back and rethink the approach with AI as the organising principle rather than an afterthought, according to the people familiar with the discussions.

What Lighthouse Would Look Like

The project encompasses a broad set of features that use AI to improve how viewers discover films and television shows. The system would learn consumer preferences over time and respond to spoken requests, according to one person with knowledge of the project.

https://x.com/tmiyatake1/status/2080445355389604118

Prime Video is working on redesigning its main homepage as part of Lighthouse. One option discussed by executives includes AI-driven tiles with pre-populated viewing suggestions such as "action movies from the 1980s" or "Christmas rom-coms," according to three of the sources. Another source said a current version of the design does not include text-heavy tiles. The traditional search function would remain.

Amazon's Broader AI Ambitions

Lighthouse is viewed as one critical piece of Amazon's company-wide effort to elevate its standing in artificial intelligence as competitors race ahead. OpenAI and Anthropic have captured much of the public conversation around AI, while Amazon's own consumer-facing AI efforts have had mixed results.

The multiyear overhaul of its Alexa voice assistant to provide more conversational, AI-powered responses has progressed slowly and the unit continues to lose money, Reuters has previously reported. A successful deployment of AI across Prime Video — a platform already embedded in the daily routines of hundreds of millions of households — could offer a more compelling demonstration of Amazon's capabilities.

What's at Stake

The streaming wars have increasingly become a technology competition as much as a content one. Netflix has invested heavily in its recommendation algorithms for years, and Apple TV+ is integrating Siri-powered discovery. By making AI the backbone of Prime Video's user experience rather than a layer on top of it, Amazon would be attempting to turn its streaming service into a differentiator for its broader AI narrative.

Amazon declined to comment on the report. The final design of the redesign has not been settled, and no public launch date has been announced. But for the 200 million consumers who open Prime Video each month, the change — whenever it arrives — could fundamentally reshape how they find something to watch.
